title: SI base units of pressure (p = F/A)
subject: physics
stem:
The pressure \(p\) exerted by a force is given by
\[
p=\frac{F}{A}
\]
where \(F\) is the force and \(A\) is the area it acts on.

Using this equation, determine the SI base units of pressure.

steps.title: Unit of force
steps.prompt: What are the SI base units of force \(F\)?
steps.explanation: From \(F=ma\): \(\mathrm{kg}\times\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}\). The newton is a derived unit, not a base unit.

steps.title: Unit of area
steps.prompt: What is the SI base unit of area \(A\)?

steps.title: Unit of pressure
steps.prompt: Using \(p=\dfrac{F}{A}\), what are the SI base units of pressure?
steps.explanation: \(\dfrac{\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}}{\mathrm{m^{2}}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\). The pascal is derived, not base.

title: Homogeneity: speed of a wave on a string
subject: physics
stem:
The speed \(v\) of a transverse wave on a stretched string is given by
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
\]
where \(T\) is the tension in the string and \(\mu\) is the mass per unit length of the string.

Use SI base units to determine whether the equation is homogeneous.

steps.title: Unit of tension
steps.prompt: Tension is a force. What are the SI base units of \(T\)?

steps.title: Unit of mass per unit length
steps.prompt: What are the SI base units of \(\mu\)?

steps.title: Units inside the square root
steps.prompt: What are the SI base units of \(\dfrac{T}{\mu}\)?

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.prompt: Which statement is correct?
options: Homogeneous: both sides have units m s⁻¹
Not homogeneous: the right-hand side has units m² s⁻²
Not homogeneous: the right-hand side has units m s⁻²
Homogeneous: both sides have units m² s⁻²
steps.explanation: \(\sqrt{\mathrm{m^{2}\,s^{-2}}}=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), the same as the units of \(v\), so the equation is homogeneous.

title: SI base units of viscosity (F = 6πηrv)
subject: physics
stem:
A small sphere of radius \(r\) moving at speed \(v\) through a liquid experiences a drag force \(F\) given by
\[
F=6\pi\eta r v
\]
where \(\eta\) is the viscosity of the liquid.

Determine the SI base units of \(\eta\).

steps.title: Rearrange for η
steps.prompt: Rearrange the equation to make \(\eta\) the subject.
steps.explanation: Divide both sides by \(6\pi r v\).

steps.title: Units of rv
steps.prompt: What are the SI base units of the product \(rv\)?

steps.title: Units of η
steps.prompt: What are the SI base units of \(\eta\)?

title: SI base units of capacitance (E = ½CV²)
subject: physics
stem:
The energy \(E\) stored in a capacitor is given by
\[
E=\tfrac{1}{2}CV^{2}
\]
where \(C\) is the capacitance and \(V\) is the potential difference across it.

Determine the SI base units of \(C\).

steps.title: Unit of potential difference
steps.prompt: Potential difference \(V=\dfrac{P}{I}\). What are the SI base units of \(V\)?

subSteps.title: Unit of power
subSteps.prompt: What are the SI base units of power \(P\)?

subSteps.title: Unit of current
subSteps.prompt: What is the SI base unit of current \(I\)?
subSteps.explanation: The ampere is one of the SI base units.

steps.title: Unit of energy
steps.prompt: What are the SI base units of energy \(E\)?

steps.title: Units of capacitance
steps.prompt: Using \(C=\dfrac{2E}{V^{2}}\), what are the SI base units of \(C\)?
steps.explanation: \(V^{2}\) has units \(\mathrm{kg^{2}\,m^{4}\,s^{-6}\,A^{-2}}\). Dividing: \(\dfrac{\mathrm{kg\,m^{2}\,s^{-2}}}{\mathrm{kg^{2}\,m^{4}\,s^{-6}\,A^{-2}}}=\mathrm{kg^{-1}\,m^{-2}\,s^{4}\,A^{2}}\). (\(\mathrm{A\,s}\) comes from forgetting to square \(V\).)

title: Prefixes: power of a laser pulse
subject: physics
stem:
A laser emits a single pulse of energy \(3.6\,\mathrm{mJ}\). The pulse lasts for \(12\,\mathrm{ns}\).

Calculate the average power of the pulse.

steps.title: Convert the energy
steps.prompt: What is \(3.6\,\mathrm{mJ}\) in joules?

steps.title: Convert the time
steps.prompt: What is \(12\,\mathrm{ns}\) in seconds?

steps.title: Calculate the power
steps.prompt: What is the average power of the pulse?

title: Uncertainty: length of a rod on a rule
subject: physics
stem:
A student uses a rule marked in millimetres to measure the length of a rod, as shown.

The left end of the rod is at the \(2.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) mark and the right end is at the \(14.6\,\mathrm{cm}\) mark. Each reading on the rule has an uncertainty of \(\pm0.05\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Determine the length of the rod and its percentage uncertainty.

steps.title: Length of the rod
steps.prompt: What is the length of the rod?

steps.title: Absolute uncertainty
steps.prompt: What is the absolute uncertainty in the length?
steps.explanation: The length comes from two readings, so the uncertainties add: \(0.05+0.05=0.1\,\mathrm{cm}\).

steps.title: Percentage uncertainty
steps.prompt: What is the percentage uncertainty in the length?

title: Uncertainty: density of a cylinder
subject: physics
stem:
The density \(\rho\) of a solid cylinder is found using
\[
\rho=\frac{4m}{\pi d^{2}h}
\]
The measurements are:
- mass \(m=(48.0\pm0.5)\,\mathrm{g}\)
- diameter \(d=(2.50\pm0.02)\,\mathrm{cm}\)
- height \(h=(4.00\pm0.05)\,\mathrm{cm}\)

Determine the percentage uncertainty in \(\rho\).

steps.title: Percentage uncertainty in m
steps.prompt: What is the percentage uncertainty in \(m\)?

steps.title: Contribution from d
steps.prompt: \(d\) is squared in the equation. What is the percentage uncertainty contributed by \(d^{2}\)?

steps.title: Total percentage uncertainty
steps.prompt: What is the percentage uncertainty in \(\rho\)?
steps.explanation: Add the percentages: \(1.04+1.6+1.25=3.9\%\). The constants \(4\) and \(\pi\) have no uncertainty.

title: Uncertainty: period from timing 20 oscillations
subject: physics
stem:
A student uses a stopwatch to time 20 complete oscillations of a pendulum. The time recorded is \((16.4\pm0.2)\,\mathrm{s}\).

Determine the period of the pendulum and its percentage uncertainty.

steps.title: Period
steps.prompt: What is the period \(T\) of the pendulum?

steps.title: Absolute uncertainty in T
steps.prompt: What is the absolute uncertainty in \(T\)?
steps.explanation: The uncertainty is shared over the 20 oscillations: \(\dfrac{0.2}{20}=0.01\,\mathrm{s}\).

steps.title: Percentage uncertainty
steps.prompt: What is the percentage uncertainty in \(T\)?

title: Uncertainty: g from a pendulum
subject: physics
stem:
The acceleration of free fall \(g\) is found using a simple pendulum and the equation
\[
g=\frac{4\pi^{2}L}{T^{2}}
\]
The measurements are:
- length \(L=(0.800\pm0.004)\,\mathrm{m}\)
- period \(T=(1.80\pm0.02)\,\mathrm{s}\)

Determine \(g\) with its absolute uncertainty.

steps.title: Value of g
steps.prompt: What is the value of \(g\) calculated from these measurements?
steps.explanation: \(g=\dfrac{4\pi^{2}\times0.800}{1.80^{2}}=9.75\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Use the measurements, not the textbook value.

steps.title: Percentage uncertainty in g
steps.prompt: What is the percentage uncertainty in \(g\)?

steps.title: Final answer
steps.prompt: How should \(g\) be written with its absolute uncertainty?
steps.explanation: \(\Delta g=0.027\times9.75=0.26\), given to 1 s.f. as \(0.3\). The value is then rounded to the same decimal place: \(9.7\).

title: Systematic error: zero error on an ammeter
subject: physics
stem:
An analogue ammeter is used to measure the current in a circuit.

The diagram shows the meter before it is connected, when there is no current, and then when it is connected in the circuit.

steps.title: Type of error
steps.prompt: What type of error does the left-hand meter show?
steps.explanation: The pointer reads \(0.2\,\mathrm{A}\) when there is no current. Every reading is too large by the same amount, which is a systematic zero error.

steps.title: Corrected current
steps.prompt: What is the actual current in the circuit?

steps.title: Effect of repeat readings
steps.prompt: The student takes many repeat readings and calculates the mean. What happens to this error?
steps.explanation: Averaging only reduces random errors. A systematic error shifts every reading by the same amount, so the mean is still wrong by \(0.2\,\mathrm{A}\).

title: Vectors: components of a pulling force
subject: physics
stem:
A crate on a horizontal floor is pulled by a rope. The tension in the rope is \(40\,\mathrm{N}\) and the rope is at \(30^{\circ}\) to the horizontal, as shown.

Determine the horizontal and vertical components of the tension.

steps.title: Pick the expression
steps.prompt: Which expression gives the horizontal component of the tension?
steps.explanation: The horizontal component is adjacent to the \(30^{\circ}\) angle, so it uses cosine.

steps.title: Horizontal component
steps.prompt: What is the horizontal component?

steps.title: Vertical component
steps.prompt: What is the vertical component?

title: Vectors: resultant of two forces at 60°
subject: physics
stem:
Two forces act at point O. One force of \(5.0\,\mathrm{N}\) acts horizontally. The other force of \(3.0\,\mathrm{N}\) acts at \(60^{\circ}\) to the first force, as shown.

Determine the magnitude of the resultant force.

steps.title: Total horizontal component
steps.prompt: What is the total horizontal component of the two forces?

steps.title: Total vertical component
steps.prompt: What is the total vertical component?
steps.explanation: Only the \(3.0\,\mathrm{N}\) force has a vertical part: \(3.0\sin60^{\circ}=2.6\,\mathrm{N}\).

steps.title: Resultant
steps.prompt: What is the magnitude of the resultant force?
steps.explanation: \(R=\sqrt{6.5^{2}+2.6^{2}}=7.0\,\mathrm{N}\). The forces are not perpendicular, so \(\sqrt{5^{2}+3^{2}}\) is wrong.

title: Vectors: boat crossing a river
subject: physics
stem:
A river is \(45\,\mathrm{m}\) wide and the water flows parallel to the banks at \(1.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

A boat is pointed straight across the river, at right angles to the banks. Its speed relative to the water is \(3.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Determine how far downstream the boat lands.

steps.title: Resultant speed
steps.prompt: What is the speed of the boat relative to the banks?

steps.title: Time to cross
steps.prompt: How long does the boat take to cross the river?
steps.explanation: Only the velocity component across the river matters: \(t=\dfrac{45}{3.0}=15\,\mathrm{s}\). The current does not change this.

steps.title: Distance downstream
steps.prompt: How far downstream does the boat land?

title: Vectors: change in velocity at a corner
subject: physics
stem:
A car travels due north at \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). After turning a corner, it travels due east at \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Determine the change in velocity of the car.

steps.title: Set up the subtraction
steps.prompt: Change in velocity \(=\) final velocity \(-\) initial velocity. Subtracting a vector is the same as adding its reverse. Which two vectors must be added?
options: 20 m s⁻¹ east and 15 m s⁻¹ north
20 m s⁻¹ east and 15 m s⁻¹ south
20 m s⁻¹ west and 15 m s⁻¹ north
20 m s⁻¹ east and 15 m s⁻¹ east
steps.explanation: \(\Delta\vec v=\vec v_{\text{final}}+(-\vec v_{\text{initial}})\). The reverse of 15 north is 15 south.

steps.title: Magnitude
steps.prompt: What is the magnitude of the change in velocity?

steps.title: Direction
steps.prompt: What is the direction of the change in velocity?

title: Kinematics: v–t graph of a car journey
subject: physics
stem: The velocity–time graph shows a car journey along a straight road. The car accelerates uniformly from rest, travels at constant velocity, and then decelerates uniformly to rest at \(t=13\,\mathrm{s}\).

steps.title: Acceleration
steps.prompt: What is the acceleration of the car during the first \(4.0\,\mathrm{s}\)?

steps.title: Total distance
steps.prompt: What is the total distance travelled?
steps.explanation: Distance is the area under the graph: \(\tfrac12(4)(12)+(6)(12)+\tfrac12(3)(12)=24+72+18=114\,\mathrm{m}\).

steps.title: Average speed
steps.prompt: What is the average speed for the whole journey?
steps.explanation: \(\dfrac{114}{13}=8.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Divide by the total time, including the time spent accelerating and braking.

title: Kinematics: stopping distance of a car
subject: physics
stem:
A driver is travelling at \(25\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) when they see a hazard ahead. The driver's reaction time is \(0.60\,\mathrm{s}\). The driver then brakes, and the car decelerates uniformly at \(5.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) until it stops.

Calculate the total stopping distance.

steps.title: Thinking distance
steps.prompt: How far does the car travel during the reaction time?
steps.explanation: The car is still at constant speed: \(25\times0.60=15\,\mathrm{m}\).

steps.title: Braking distance
steps.prompt: How far does the car travel while braking?

steps.title: Stopping distance
steps.prompt: What is the total stopping distance?

title: Kinematics: ball kicked horizontally from a cliff
subject: physics
stem:
A ball is kicked horizontally at \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) from the top of a cliff \(45\,\mathrm{m}\) above the sea, as shown. Air resistance is negligible.

Take \(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

steps.title: What sets the time
steps.prompt: Which quantity determines how long the ball is in the air?
options: the horizontal speed of 12 m s⁻¹
the vertical motion: starting from zero vertical velocity and falling 45 m
both the horizontal speed and the height
steps.explanation: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent. The ball starts with no vertical velocity, so only the fall of \(45\,\mathrm{m}\) matters.

steps.title: Time of flight
steps.prompt: How long does the ball take to reach the sea?

steps.title: Horizontal distance
steps.prompt: How far from the foot of the cliff does the ball land?

steps.title: Impact speed
steps.prompt: What is the speed of the ball as it hits the sea?

title: Kinematics: ball thrown up from a roof
subject: physics
stem:
A ball is thrown vertically upwards at \(14.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) from the edge of a flat roof \(20.0\,\mathrm{m}\) above the ground. It rises, then falls past the roof to the ground, as shown. Air resistance is negligible.

Take upwards as positive and \(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

steps.title: Signs of s, u and a
steps.prompt: For the whole flight from the roof to the ground, which set of values is correct?
steps.explanation: The ball ends \(20.0\,\mathrm{m}\) below where it started, it is thrown upwards, and gravity acts downwards.

steps.title: Maximum height
steps.prompt: What is the maximum height of the ball above the ground?
steps.explanation: At the top \(v=0\): \(h=\dfrac{14.0^{2}}{2\times9.81}=10.0\,\mathrm{m}\) above the roof, so \(30.0\,\mathrm{m}\) above the ground.

steps.title: Speed at the ground
steps.prompt: What is the speed of the ball just before it hits the ground?

steps.title: Time of flight
steps.prompt: How long after being thrown does the ball hit the ground?

title: Kinematics: displacement–time graph of a cyclist
subject: physics
stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a cyclist along a straight road over \(24\,\mathrm{s}\).

steps.title: Velocity in the first stage
steps.prompt: What is the velocity of the cyclist during the first \(10\,\mathrm{s}\)?

steps.title: Velocity in the last stage
steps.prompt: What is the velocity between \(t=16\,\mathrm{s}\) and \(t=24\,\mathrm{s}\)?
steps.explanation: \(\dfrac{10-50}{24-16}=-5.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The negative sign shows the cyclist is moving back towards the start.

steps.title: Average velocity
steps.prompt: What is the average velocity for the whole \(24\,\mathrm{s}\)?
steps.explanation: Average velocity \(=\dfrac{\text{final displacement}}{\text{time}}=\dfrac{10}{24}=0.42\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). \(3.75\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) is the average speed (distance \(90\,\mathrm{m}\)).

title: Kinematics: stone dropped from a bridge
subject: physics
stem:
A stone is dropped from rest from a bridge. It hits the water \(2.5\,\mathrm{s}\) later. Air resistance is negligible.

Take \(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

steps.title: Pick the equation
steps.prompt: Which equation gives the height of the bridge above the water?

steps.title: Height
steps.prompt: What is the height of the bridge above the water?

steps.title: Impact speed
steps.prompt: What is the speed of the stone as it hits the water?
